newsitem.title: USA: Dlr barely firmer vs mark, lower vs yen at US open.
newsitem.headline: Dlr barely firmer vs mark, lower vs yen at US open.

text.p: The dollar opened marginally higher versus the mark but weaker against the yen after remarks from key Japanese leaders sparked renewed concern about prospects for higher official interest rates in Japan, currency experts said.
The Bank of Japan (BOJ) has kept its official discount rate at a record low 0.5 percent since September 1995 in order to help bolster Japan's economic recovery.
Yet BOJ Governor Yasuo Matsushita told a parliamentary committee it was important to take policy steps pre-emptively in order to realize continued growth without inflation.

Separately, Taku Yamasaki, chairman of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party's (LDP) policy research council, was initially quoted by Jiji news agency as saying the option of implementing fiscal stimulus steps such as an extra budget will not be ruled out in a fiscal reform law that the Japanese government plans to draw up by the end of June. However, Yamasaki later retracted his comment.

Foreign Exchange Analytics Partner David Gilmore noted that if the Japanese government starts spending more, that would prove stimulatory. "The Bank of Japan doesn't have to carry the burden of stimulating with low interest rates."
Gilmore also cited talk of dollar selling by Japanese names and U.S. hedge funds above 116 yen.
The dollar opened at 115.62/72 yen, down from 116.28/38 yen at Wednesday's close. Against the mark, the dollar inched up to 1.7285/95 from 1.7275/85.

Foreign exchange market players also mulled over a flurry of German economic figures including news that first-quarter, pan-German gross domestic product (GDP) rose 0.5 percent on a quarter-over-quarter basis and 1.4 percent on a yearly basis versus expected gains of 0.3 percent and 2.6 percent, respectively.

Market players are also looking forward to a Franco-German summit in Poitiers, western France on June 13. French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin and President Jacques Chirac will participate in what will be the first time both attend an international meeting together since elections on Sunday.
Hillel Waxman, a first vice president at Bank Leumi Trust Co of New York, said the summit is expected to yield significant talks about what to do about the euro.
Waxman said the dollar versus European currencies remains "relatively well bid" until there is increased clarification regarding the future of the euro and the monetary structure.
Waxman said he expects the dollar to stick to current ranges on Thursday, with the assumption the dollar will try to retest above 1.73 marks.

On Friday, currency markets face the release of key U.S. employment data. Economists polled by Reuters predicted, on average, that the economy added 219,000 non-farm payroll jobs in May after picking up 142,000 in April.
The unemployment rate is seen creeping up to 5.0 percent from 4.9 percent, while average hourly earnings are expected to have risen 0.4 percent in May after falling 0.1 percent in the previous month.

Mark Gargano, managing director of currency derivatives at First Union National Bank, said he doubted non-farm payrolls will move the market as much as some people think as long as the average in the first five months stays between 200,000 to 225,000.
Then, I think, the market believes the growth level is "fairly consistent" -- not roaring ahead or slowing down dramatically, he added.
In other trade, the dollar opened at 1.4440/50 Swiss francs, up slightly from 1.4437/47 francs at the prior close.
The dollar was nearly flat at Canadian $1.3763/68 versus C$1.3764/69. The Australian dollar opened at $0.7601/06, up from $0.7576/81. -- Donna Sells 212-859-1668
